claim: Human speech and bird song are acoustically complex communication signals that are learned by imitation during a sensitive period early in life.
source: Human speech and bird song are acoustically complex communication signals that are learned by imitation during a sensitive period early in life.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about speech and song learning, supported by the citation context of the manuscript.

claim: The brain areas indispensable for speech and song learning are known.
source: Although the brain areas indispensable for speech and song learning are known, the neural circuits important for enhanced or reduced vocal performance remain unclear.
evidence: This statement refers to established knowledge in the field, as indicated by the context and subsequent citations in the manuscript.

claim: The neural circuits important for enhanced or reduced vocal performance remain unclear.
source: Although the brain areas indispensable for speech and song learning are known, the neural circuits important for enhanced or reduced vocal performance remain unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Song imitation accuracy correlates with the structural architecture of four distinct brain areas, none of which pertain to the song control system.
source: By combining in vivo structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging with song analyses in juvenile male zebra finches during song learning and beyond, we reveal that song imitation accuracy correlates with the structural architecture of four distinct brain areas, none of which pertain to the song control system.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data from MRI and song analysis.

claim: The structural properties of a secondary auditory area in the left hemisphere are capable of predicting future song copying accuracy at the earliest stages of learning, before initiating vocal practicing.
source: Furthermore, the structural properties of a secondary auditory area in the left hemisphere, are capable to predict future song copying accuracy, already at the earliest stages of learning, before initiating vocal practicing.
evidence: This is a key finding based on longitudinal MRI data and song analysis.

claim: Ultimate performance in part depends on factors experienced before vocal practicing.
source: These findings appoint novel brain regions important for song learning outcome and inform that ultimate performance in part depends on factors experienced before vocal practicing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the predictive relationship found between early brain structure and later performance.

claim: Human speech and bird song are highly complex and rapid motor behaviours that are learned by imitation from adults.
source: Human speech and bird song are highly complex and rapid motor behaviours that are learned by imitation from adults and serve to produce complex communication signals vital for social interactions (Brainard and Doupe, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brainard and Doupe, 2013.

claim: Human speech and bird song serve to produce complex communication signals vital for social interactions.
source: Human speech and bird song are highly complex and rapid motor behaviours that are learned by imitation from adults and serve to produce complex communication signals vital for social interactions (Brainard and Doupe, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brainard and Doupe, 2013.

claim: Both human speech and bird song are acquired during a temporally well-defined sensitive period early in life.
source: Both are acquired during a temporally well-defined sensitive period early in life which consists of a sensory learning phase where a perceptual target of speech sounds or a song model are memorised, followed by a sensorimotor learning phase, where human infants or juvenile birds engage in intense vocal practicing and will try to match the spectro-temporal characteristics of their own vocalisations to the previously established perceptual targets based on multi-sensory feedback (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999; Tchernichovski et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Doupe and Kuhl, 1999 and Tchernichovski et al., 2001.

claim: The sensitive period for speech and song learning consists of a sensory learning phase followed by a sensorimotor learning phase.
source: Both are acquired during a temporally well-defined sensitive period early in life which consists of a sensory learning phase where a perceptual target of speech sounds or a song model are memorised, followed by a sensorimotor learning phase, where human infants or juvenile birds engage in intense vocal practicing and will try to match the spectro-temporal characteristics of their own vocalisations to the previously established perceptual targets based on multi-sensory feedback (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999; Tchernichovski et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Doupe and Kuhl, 1999 and Tchernichovski et al., 2001.

claim: During the sensorimotor learning phase, human infants or juvenile birds engage in intense vocal practicing to match their vocalizations to previously established perceptual targets based on multi-sensory feedback.
source: Both are acquired during a temporally well-defined sensitive period early in life which consists of a sensory learning phase where a perceptual target of speech sounds or a song model are memorised, followed by a sensorimotor learning phase, where human infants or juvenile birds engage in intense vocal practicing and will try to match the spectro-temporal characteristics of their own vocalisations to the previously established perceptual targets based on multi-sensory feedback (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999; Tchernichovski et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Doupe and Kuhl, 1999 and Tchernichovski et al., 2001.

claim: Zebra finches are an established model to study certain aspects of human speech acquisition.
source: Zebra finches, an established model to study certain aspects of human speech acquisition (Brainard and Doupe, 2013), learn to sing a single song that crystallises (i.e. remains unchanged) for life after the sensorimotor learning phase.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brainard and Doupe, 2013.

claim: Zebra finches learn to sing a single song that crystallises for life after the sensorimotor learning phase.
source: Zebra finches, an established model to study certain aspects of human speech acquisition (Brainard and Doupe, 2013), learn to sing a single song that crystallises (i.e. remains unchanged) for life after the sensorimotor learning phase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebra finch song learning, supported by the citation context.

claim: The success of the song learning process can be accurately quantified by computing the acoustic similarity between the song learned and sang by the pupil and the original tutor song.
source: The success of the song learning process can be accurately quantified by computing the acoustic similarity between the song learned and sang by the pupil and the original tutor song that is used as a reference (Tchernichovski et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tchernichovski et al., 2000.

claim: Only zebra finch males learn to sing.
source: Intriguingly, only zebra finch males learn to sing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebra finch biology.

claim: Juvenile female zebra finches do not experience a sensorimotor and crystallisation phase for song learning like male zebra finches do.
source: As a result, juvenile female zebra finches do not experience a sensorimotor and crystallisation phase for song learning like male zebra finches do.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that only males sing.

claim: Female zebra finches rely on early exposure to song to form an auditory memory of tutor song to develop song preference.
source: However, female zebra finches do rely on early exposure to song to form an auditory memory of tutor song to develop song preference (Hauber et al., 2013; Bolhuis and Moorman, 2015; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hauber et al., 2013; Bolhuis and Moorman, 2015; Chen et al., 2016.

claim: In songbirds, sensory learning is thought to depend on a distributed set of areas including several auditory regions.
source: In songbirds, sensory learning is thought to depend on a distributed set of areas including several auditory regions (Bolhuis and Gahr, 2006; Hahnloser and Kotowicz, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bolhuis and Gahr, 2006 and Hahnloser and Kotowicz, 2010.

claim: The motor aspect of song is encoded by cortical areas.
source: The motor aspect of song is encoded by cortical areas (Wild, 1997), which receive input from the vocal basal ganglia to introduce variability in vocal motor output during sensorimotor practicing (Bottjer et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wild, 1997 and Bottjer et al., 1984.

claim: Cortical areas encoding song motor aspects receive input from the vocal basal ganglia to introduce variability in vocal motor output during sensorimotor practicing.
source: The motor aspect of song is encoded by cortical areas (Wild, 1997), which receive input from the vocal basal ganglia to introduce variability in vocal motor output during sensorimotor practicing (Bottjer et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bottjer et al., 1984.

claim: Auditory feedback signals that encode errors in own performance were detected in the secondary auditory areas.
source: Auditory feedback signals that encode errors in own performance were detected in the secondary auditory areas (Keller and Hahnloser, 2009) and are likely transmitted to the dopaminergic midbrain nuclei (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2014), via the ventral pallidum (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Keller and Hahnloser, 2009; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2014; and Chen et al., 2019.

claim: The dopaminergic midbrain nuclei and ventral pallidum steer vocalisations towards the desired vocal target during sensorimotor song learning.
source: The dopaminergic midbrain nuclei and ventral pallidum were recently found to steer vocalisations towards the desired vocal target during sensorimotor song learning (Hisey et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hisey et al., 2018 and Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Each of the song learning pathways is indispensable for sensorimotor learning to succeed.
source: Each of these pathways is indispensable for sensorimotor learning to succeed, and during the sensorimotor learning phase, the precise interplay of these systems is tightly set.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature about song learning pathways.

claim: The song control system is more enhanced in male zebra finches compared to females.
source: Furthermore, the behavioural difference between male and female zebra finches (only males sing) is reflected in the structural organisation of the zebra finch brain. That is, the song control system, a circuitry composed of well-delineated brain areas that are interconnected by fibre pathways and that are responsible for singing behaviour, is more enhanced in males compared to females (MacDougall-Shackleton and Ball, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to MacDougall-Shackleton and Ball, 1999.

claim: Structural differences between male and female zebra finches include disparities in local volume, interconnectivity as well as intrinsic microstructural tissue properties.
source: These structural differences include disparities in local volume, interconnectivity as well as intrinsic microstructural tissue properties (e.g. soma size of LMAN) (Nixdorf-Bergweiler, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nixdorf-Bergweiler, 1998.

claim: The differences between male and female birds in volume of the song control system nuclei arise during the song learning period.
source: The differences between male and female birds in volume of the song control system nuclei arise during the song learning period (when juvenile males actively engage in vocal motor practicing [Nixdorf-Bergweiler, 1996].
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nixdorf-Bergweiler, 1996.

claim: Live tutoring results in higher song similarity scores compared to what is achieved by tape tutored birds.
source: For example, live tutoring results in higher song similarity scores compared to what is achieved by tape tutored birds (Derégnaucourt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Derégnaucourt et al., 2013.

claim: Social feedback that juveniles receive from adult zebra finches during the sensory and sensorimotor period of vocal learning is capable of influencing song learning accuracy levels.
source: Social feedback that juveniles receive from the adult male and female zebra finch (its caretakers) during the sensory and sensorimotor period of vocal learning is capable of influencing song learning accuracy levels (Chen et al., 2016; Carouso-Peck and Goldstein, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016 and Carouso-Peck and Goldstein, 2019.

claim: Additional brain areas and neural circuits outside the traditionally studied auditory and song control system may be involved and capable of influencing ultimate song performance levels.
source: Therefore, it is expected that additional brain areas and neural circuits outside the traditionally studied auditory and song control system may be involved and perhaps are capable of influencing ultimate song performance (i.e. learning accuracy) levels.
evidence: This is a hypothesis or expectation based on the evidence about social factors in song learning.

claim: Sex differences in local tissue microstructure exclusively co-localise with the song control nuclei and arise along the song learning process.
source: Using voxel-based statistical testing, we established spatio-temporal maps that revealed that (1) sex differences in local tissue microstructure exclusively co-localise with the song control nuclei and arise along the song learning process, and (2) most myelin-containing brain structures exhibit structural maturational changes between 20 and 200 dph.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's voxel-based statistical analysis of MRI data.

claim: Most myelin-containing brain structures exhibit structural maturational changes between 20 and 200 dph.
source: Using voxel-based statistical testing, we established spatio-temporal maps that revealed that (1) sex differences in local tissue microstructure exclusively co-localise with the song control nuclei and arise along the song learning process, and (2) most myelin-containing brain structures exhibit structural maturational changes between 20 and 200 dph.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's voxel-based statistical analysis of MRI data.

claim: The structural properties of specific parts of the secondary auditory cortices (left NCM and CM), the ventral pallidum (VP), and the fronto-arcopallial tract (tFA) correlate with song imitation accuracy.
source: Likewise, we discovered that the structural properties of specific parts of the secondary auditory cortices, that is left caudomedial nidopallium (NCM) and the caudomedial mesopallium (CM), and unexpectedly, the ventral pallidum (VP) and the fronto-arcopallial tract (tFA) correlate with song imitation accuracy, while the different nuclei of the SCS seemed not involved.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the voxel-based correlational analyses.

claim: The different nuclei of the song control system (SCS) seemed not involved in correlations with song imitation accuracy.
source: Likewise, we discovered that the structural properties of specific parts of the secondary auditory cortices, that is left caudomedial nidopallium (NCM) and the caudomedial mesopallium (CM), and unexpectedly, the ventral pallidum (VP) and the fronto-arcopallial tract (tFA) correlate with song imitation accuracy, while the different nuclei of the SCS seemed not involved.
evidence: This is a finding from the voxel-based correlational analyses.

claim: The structural properties of left NCM and the tFA mainly reflect relationships between performance and structure at the population-level.
source: Indepth analyses revealed that the structural properties of left NCM and the tFA mainly reflect relationships between performance and structure at the population-level, while the structural architecture of the CM and VP appears to change along the sensorimotor learning process, in individual birds.
evidence: This is based on in-depth correlation analyses distinguishing between-subject and within-subject effects.

claim: The structural architecture of the CM and VP appears to change along the sensorimotor learning process, in individual birds.
source: Indepth analyses revealed that the structural properties of left NCM and the tFA mainly reflect relationships between performance and structure at the population-level, while the structural architecture of the CM and VP appears to change along the sensorimotor learning process, in individual birds.
evidence: This is based on repeated-measures correlation analyses.

claim: The structural properties of left NCM are predictive of future learning accuracy already before pupils actively engage in vocal practicing during the early phases of sensory learning.
source: Fascinatingly, we also discovered that the structural properties of left NCM are predictive of future learning accuracy already before pupils actively engage in vocal practicing during the early phases of sensory learning.
evidence: This is a finding from analyses comparing good and bad learners at early time points.

claim: An interaction between age and sex for Fractional Anisotropy (FA) was detected in clusters bilateral at the Area X surroundings and the arcopallium.
source: Such an interaction was detected in clusters bilateral at the Area X surroundings and the arcopallium (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is based on voxel-based repeated measures ANOVA on DTI data, as shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Most myelin containing structures and lamina of the juvenile zebra finch brain mature between 20 and 200 dph.
source: The data illustrate that most myelin containing structures and lamina of the juvenile zebra finch brain mature between 20 and 200 dph (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on the main effect of age analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The duration of the inter-syllable intervals gradually shortens from sensorimotor to song crystallisation and even after song crystallisation towards 200 dph.
source: The duration of the inter-syllable intervals gradually shortens from sensorimotor to song crystallisation and even after song crystallisation towards 200 dph (p<0.0001 F(3, 38.2)=13.8789; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of song recordings.

claim: Birds gradually sing faster as they mature.
source: This indicates that birds gradually sing faster.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that inter-syllable intervals shorten over time.

claim: Syllable Wiener entropy scores decrease during the sensorimotor phase.
source: Syllable Wiener entropy scores decrease during the sensorimotor phase (p=0.0032 F(3, 37.8)=5.48; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), meaning that the syllables gain in tonality.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of song recordings, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Syllables are sung with lower acoustic variability when song crystallises between 90 and 120 dph.
source: Further, by quantifying the standard deviation of the spectro-temporal features, we observe that syllables are sung with lower acoustic variability when song crystallises between 90 and 120 dph (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of song variability shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The syllables gain tonality, become more structured, and less acoustically diverse along sensorimotor song maturation.
source: These analyses informed that the syllables gain tonality (lower acoustic noisiness), become more structured (less noisy) and less acoustically diverse along sensorimotor song maturation.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the song analysis data.

claim: While the spectral content of syllables mainly forms during the sensorimotor phase, the temporal properties of the songs continue to change beyond the crystallisation phase.
source: Furthermore, while the spectral content of syllables mainly forms during the sensorimotor phase, the temporal properties of the songs continue to change beyond the crystallisation phase.
evidence: This is an inference from the song analysis data showing different trajectories for spectral and temporal features.

claim: Song similarity to tutor song increased gradually from 65 to 200 dph.
source: Song similarity to tutor song increased gradually from 65 to 200 dph (p=0.0251 F(3, 37.0)=3.4890; Figure 2A) reaching similar levels as described by others (Tchernichovski et al., 2000; Derégnaucourt and Gahr, 2013).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of song similarity scores shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sequence stereotypy increased gradually from 65 to 200 dph.
source: Moreover, as song crystallisation results in a highly stereotyped, consistent order of syllables within a motif, sequence stereotypy also increased gradually from 65 to 200 dph (p=0.0052 F(3, 38.4)=4.7904, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of sequence stereotypy shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Song similarity is dependent on tutor identity.
source: Consistent with this, we observed that song similarity depended on tutor identity, that is, juveniles will consistently sing a good or less good tutor song copy depending on their tutor (p=0.0159 F(7,6.1)=6.7597; Figure 2A – colours reflect tutor identity).
evidence: This is based on mixed-effect model analysis with tutor identity as a factor.

claim: Correlations between song similarity and FA were observed in the left tFA.
source: Correlations between song similarity and FA were observed in the left tFA (peak: pFWE <0.001 T = 6.81; Figure 3A), and in left NCM (rostral NCM; peak: pFWE = 0.019 T = 5.69; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on voxel-based multiple regression analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Correlations between song similarity and FA were observed in left NCM.
source: Correlations between song similarity and FA were observed in the left tFA (peak: pFWE <0.001 T = 6.81; Figure 3A), and in left NCM (rostral NCM; peak: pFWE = 0.019 T = 5.69; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on voxel-based multiple regression analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A cluster was found midsagittal near the striatum and mesopallium, extending laterally and caudo-ventrally adjacent to the septomesencephalic tract, identified as the VP.
source: Furthermore, we found an additional cluster midsagittal near the striatum and mesopallium, extending laterally and caudo-ventrally adjacent to the septomesencephalic tract (TSM; sub-peak next to the TSM in the left hemisphere: pFWE = 0.002 T = 6.38; Figure 3C). Based on this spatial pattern and in accordance with the Karten-Mitra zebra finch brain atlas (http://www.zebrafinchatlas.org/; Karten et al., 2013), we identified this area as the VP.
evidence: This is based on voxel-based analysis and anatomical identification using an atlas.

claim: At a less conservative threshold, clusters could be observed at the right tFA and the right NCM.
source: Interestingly, when inspecting the statistical maps at a less conservative threshold (puncorrected <0.001 kE ≥40 voxels), clusters could be also observed at the right tFA (peak: pFWE = 0.001 T = 6.42) and the right NCM (peak: pFWE = 0.032 T = 5.55; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is based on voxel-based analysis at a different threshold.

claim: The cluster covering the left NCM extends rostro-laterally towards the CM.
source: Also at this less conservative threshold, we observe that the cluster covering the left NCM extends rostro-laterally towards the CM (sub-peak of NCM cluster: pFWE = 0.194 T = 5.01; Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on voxel-based analysis shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Learning accuracy anticorrelates with local volume in the VP and the CM.
source: To test if learning accuracy correlates with the local volume of specific brain areas (log mwj), we performed voxel-based analysis and found a significant anticorrelation in two brain areas, that is the VP (peak: pFWE <0.001 T = 8.06; Figure 4A) and the medial and lateral portions of the CM rostral to field L (resp. CMM and CLM) potentially including nucleus avalanche (Av; left: peak: pFWE = 0.001 T = 7.10; right: peak: pFWE <0.001 T = 7.42; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on voxel-based analysis of local volume shown in Figure 4A and 4C.

claim: Birds that sing a better copy of the tutor song have higher FA values in NCM, the VP and the tFA, both during the sensorimotor phase as well as after song crystallisation.
source: Together, these findings suggest that birds that sing a better copy of the tutor song have higher FA values in NCM, the VP and the tFA, both during the sensorimotor phase as well as after song crystallisation.
evidence: This is an inference from the Spearman correlation analyses at specific time points.

claim: Learning-related individual advances in producing a more accurate acoustic copy of the tutor song correlate with local tissue structure in the caudal mesopallium and VP.
source: Furthermore, learning-related individual advances in producing a more accurate acoustic copy of the tutor song correlate with local tissue structure in the caudal mesopallium and VP.
evidence: This is based on repeated-measures correlation analyses.

claim: Higher song similarity is related to a smaller volume of the VP and CM or a higher FA in the VP, tFA and NCM.
source: Overall, higher song similarity is related to a smaller volume of the VP and CM or a higher FA (more ordered structure) in the VP, tFA and NCM.
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation findings.

claim: No correlations could be observed between song similarity and the structural properties of the song control system nuclei (HVC, Area X, LMAN, RA).
source: Then, we tested for correlations between the structural readouts and song similarity. No correlations could be observed (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on ROI-based correlation analyses shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ultimate song performance level is determined by a complex set of circuits that synapse onto the song control system.
source: This shows that although the song control system might than be responsible for enabling song learning, the ultimate song performance level (% similarity with tutor song) is determined by a complex sets of circuits that synapse onto the song control system.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of correlation between song control system structure and performance.

claim: Future good learners consistently demonstrated higher FA values in left NCM compared to bad learners already at the earliest stages of the sensory learning phase.
source: To our surprise, future good learners consistently demonstrated higher FA values in left NCM compared to bad learners already at the earliest stages of the sensory learning phase.
evidence: This is based on analysis comparing good and bad learners at early time points (20-40 dph).

claim: FA in the left NCM displayed a significant main effect of learning accuracy (good versus bad) already at the ages 20–40 dph.
source: Interestingly, FA in the left NCM displayed a significant main effect of learning accuracy (good versus bad) already at the ages 20–40 dph (p<0.0001 F(1, 12.3)=39.2690; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on mixed-effect model analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: FA in left NCM at 20 dph was positively correlated to the % song similarity at 200 dph.
source: Furthermore, FA in left NCM at 20 dph was positively correlated (p=0.01, ρ = 0.662) to the % song similarity at 200 dph (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The structural properties of left NCM are predictive of future song copying accuracy already at 20 dph, before the juvenile finches engage in vocal practicing.
source: Thus, this structural signature is already present much before the juvenile finches engage in vocal practicing, when the pupils have been exposed to their tutor for several days (Immelmann, 1969).
evidence: This is an inference from the predictive relationship found at 20 dph.

claim: The structural properties of left NCM during the sensory phase were different in birds that in the future would become good or bad song learners.
source: While the structural properties of left NCM already appear to differentiate between future good and bad performing birds in the sensory phase, the local volume and/or intrinsic tissue properties of the VP and tFA are not different between birds with a differential future learning outcome.
evidence: This is based on the analysis comparing good and bad learners at early time points.

claim: The local volume and/or intrinsic tissue properties of the VP and tFA are not different between birds with a differential future learning outcome during the sensory phase.
source: While the structural properties of left NCM already appear to differentiate between future good and bad performing birds in the sensory phase, the local volume and/or intrinsic tissue properties of the VP and tFA are not different between birds with a differential future learning outcome.
evidence: This is based on the analysis comparing good and bad learners at early time points.

claim: The local volume of the CM and VP decreases when birds progressively become better at singing the tutor song.
source: Furthermore, the local volume of the CM and VP decreases when birds progressively become better at singing the tutor song.
evidence: This is based on repeated-measures correlation analyses.

claim: The structural properties of the CM, VP and tFA change along the sensorimotor phase.
source: These findings suggest that the structural properties of the CM, VP and tFA change along the sensorimotor phase.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation patterns observed.

claim: The CM is reciprocally connected with NCM.
source: More specifically, the CM is reciprocally connected with NCM (Vates et al., 1996) and presents clear song-selective responses (Bauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vates et al., 1996 and Bauer et al., 2008.

claim: The CM presents clear song-selective responses.
source: More specifically, the CM is reciprocally connected with NCM (Vates et al., 1996) and presents clear song-selective responses (Bauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bauer et al., 2008.

claim: Nucleus Avalanche (Av) exhibits singing-driven IEG expression that correlates with the amount of singing in normally hearing and in deafened birds.
source: A specific sub-field within the CM, the nucleus Avalanche (Av) exhibits singing-driven IEG expression that correlates with the amount of singing in normally hearing and in deafened birds (Jarvis and Nottebohm, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jarvis and Nottebohm, 1997.

claim: Av-projecting HVC neurons convey premotor signals to the Av.
source: Av-projecting HVC neurons convey premotor signals to the Av and genetic ablation of HVCAv neurons after sensory learning significantly impairs sensorimotor learning in juvenile male zebra finches (Roberts et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roberts et al., 2017.

claim: Genetic ablation of HVCAv neurons after sensory learning significantly impairs sensorimotor learning in juvenile male zebra finches.
source: Av-projecting HVC neurons convey premotor signals to the Av and genetic ablation of HVCAv neurons after sensory learning significantly impairs sensorimotor learning in juvenile male zebra finches (Roberts et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roberts et al., 2017.

claim: The CM is a prime target capable of comparing own song performance towards pre-set performance goals such as the memorised tutor song.
source: In sum, its song selective neural responses (Bauer et al., 2008), its reciprocal connectivity with NCM (Vates et al., 1996), and premotor input from HVC (Roberts et al., 2017) that might participate in the generation of error-detection signals (Keller and Hahnloser, 2009), set the CM as prime target capable of comparing own song performance towards pre-set performance goals such as the memorised tutor song.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple cited studies about CM function.

claim: The VP carries neuronal projections from the arcopallium to dopaminergic midbrain nuclei.
source: Gale et al. (2008) identified that the VP carries (i) neuronal projections from the arcopallium to dopaminergic midbrain nuclei –a pathway important in error-detection and correction mechanisms necessary for sensorimotor learning (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2014)– and (ii) axonal collaterals of the DLM-projecting Area X cells –that make up the basal ganglia-thalamic component of the song control system– project to the VP where they synapse onto VTA/SNc projecting neurons (Gale and Perkel, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gale et al., 2008 and Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2014.

claim: Dopaminergic Area X projecting VTA neurons are indispensable for sensorimotor song learning in ontogeny.
source: Using optogenetic neuromodulation, a recent study found mechanistic evidence that these dopaminergic Area X projecting VTA neurons are indispensable for sensorimotor song learning in ontogeny (Hisey et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hisey et al., 2018.

claim: VP neurons signal performance error during singing.
source: Furthermore, VP neurons signal performance error during singing and lesioning VP in juvenile male zebra finches significantly impairs song learning (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Lesioning VP in juvenile male zebra finches significantly impairs song learning.
source: Furthermore, VP neurons signal performance error during singing and lesioning VP in juvenile male zebra finches significantly impairs song learning (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Neurons located in the VP send cholinergic projections to HVC and RA.
source: Neurons located in the VP send cholinergic projections to two cortical regions responsible for the motor aspects of singing, that is HVC and RA (Li and Sakaguchi, 1997), and are capable of suppressing HVCs' neural responses to birds' own song by manipulation of the cholinergic projection neurons originating from the VP (Shea and Margoliash, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li and Sakaguchi, 1997 and Shea and Margoliash, 2003.

claim: The VP appears to be an important integration centre where several pathways converge.
source: In sum, the VP appears an important integration centre, where several pathways converge and perhaps form a closed loop system where dopaminergic midbrain nuclei can affect the basal ganglia to affect song output and vice versa, or cholinergic projections affect premotor cortical nuclei HVC and RA, based on error-signals originating from upstream auditory cortices (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple cited studies about VP connectivity and function.

claim: The volume and organization of fibres of passage in the VP becomes rearranged when birds achieve higher song copying accuracy levels.
source: Our findings clearly complement functional studies by showing that the volume and most probably the organisation of fibres of passage becomes rearranged when birds achieve higher song copying accuracy levels.
evidence: This is an inference from the MRI findings about VP structure and song accuracy.

claim: Extended training leads to decreased number of task-activated neurons in the sensorimotor striatum in mammals.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Ashby et al., 2010.

claim: The vocal basal ganglia circuitry appears more important for initial song learning but functionally disengages with producing well-learned songs after song crystallisation.
source: Also in birds, the vocal basal ganglia circuitry appears more important for initial song learning but functionally disengages with producing well-learned songs after song crystallisation (Doupe et al., 2005).

claim: The tFA carries projections from the basorostral nucleus in the rostral forebrain to the lateral arcopallium and caudolateral nidopallium.
source: The tFA carries projections from the basorostral nucleus in the rostral forebrain to the lateral arcopallium and caudolateral nidopallium. More specifically, the basorostral nucleus sends somatosensory and auditory information to the lateral arcopallium (Wild and Farabaugh, 1996), which in turn projects to jaw premotor neurons and vocal and respiratory effectors (Wild and Krützfeldt, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wild and Farabaugh, 1996 and Wild and Krützfeldt, 2012.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Tremblay et al., 2003 and Ito et al., 2009.

claim: The observation that mainly the left rather than the right NCM presents a correlation between tissue microstructure and tutor song imitation accuracy is reminiscent of leftward lateralisation of speech and language processing in humans.
source: Intriguingly, our observation that mainly the left rather than the right NCM presents a correlation between tissue microstructure and tutor song imitation accuracy (Figure 3E–H and Figure 6B–C) is reminiscent of leftward lateralisation of speech and language processing in humans (Bishop, 2013), and is consistent with a recently discovered asymmetry in tissue microstructure in the planum temporale (related to auditory speech processing) in human subjects (Ocklenburg et al., 2018), likewise measured by diffusion MRI.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the study's findings to human speech lateralization, supported by citations.
